name: C# and DotNET
scope: A person with BASIC proficiency level in C# and DotNET as a competency should be able to write and structure simple C# programs using correct syntax, namespaces, classes, and the `Main` entry point; use variables, control flow (`if`, `switch`, loops), operators, and follow .NET naming conventions; understand built-in types (numeric, string, bool, DateTime), value vs reference types, arrays, type casting, and basic memory management (stack, heap, garbage collection, IDisposable); apply basic OOP (classes, inheritance, interfaces, encapsulation, access modifiers), use common collections (`List<T>`, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>`, arrays), perform LINQ queries with basic operators and lambdas; handle exceptions (`try/catch/finally`), use and create simple custom exceptions, validate inputs, and debug with IDE tools; work with delegates, events, `Action`, `Func`, subscribe/unsubscribe events, and recognize simple functional constructs; use `async/await` for basic asynchronous programming, understand tasks, avoid blocking, and have basic awareness of threading; understand the .NET runtime, CLR, assemblies (DLL/EXE), namespaces, project/solution structure, references, and .NET Standard; build simple console apps, know basics of ASP.NET Core (middleware, routing, controllers, HTTP responses), and WinForms/WPF (forms, controls, data binding); perform basic data access using ADO.NET (`SqlConnection`, `SqlCommand`, `SqlDataReader`), parameterized queries, and Entity Framework Core for simple CRUD and migrations; read configuration from JSON/environment, use `ILogger`, manage secrets, and adapt to environments; understand dependency injection, register and resolve services in ASP.NET Core, manage dependencies via interfaces; apply basic layering, code quality, SOLID (esp. SRP, ISP), refactor, participate in code reviews, and write maintainable code; write and run basic unit tests (xUnit/NUnit/MSTest), use mocks/stubs, distinguish unit vs integration tests, and maintain tests; use Visual Studio/VS Code and dotnet CLI for build, run, test, manage NuGet packages, build configs, and static analysis; use Git for source control, branching, merging, pull requests, resolve conflicts, write XML docs, basic README, and use work tracking tools for collaboration.

{"sections":[{"name":"C# Language Basics and Syntax","scope_included":"- Understand and correctly use basic C# program structure:
  - `namespace`, `class`, `static void Main` entry point, using directives
  - File organization and relationship between files, namespaces, and assemblies
- Use fundamental C# syntax constructs:
  - Variable declarations, initialization, and scope
  - Control flow: `if` / `else`, `switch`, `while`, `do` / `while`, `for`, `foreach`
  - Basic operators: arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, null-coalescing, conditional (`?:`)
- Apply C# naming conventions and code formatting consistent with common .NET style guidelines
- Differentiate and use:
  - `using` directives vs `using` statements (for `IDisposable` resources) at a basic level
  - `var` vs explicit typing and know when each is appropriate
- Work with string handling in C#:
  - String concatenation, interpolation, and formatting
  - String comparison basics and culture-invariant comparison awareness
  - Basic usage of `StringBuilder` for repeated concatenation scenarios
- Understand and use basic C# language features:
  - Properties (auto-implemented and backing fields)
  - Constructors and object initialization syntax
  - Enums and constants (`const`, `readonly`)
  - Basic `struct` usage for simple value objects
- Understand compilation basics:
  - What compiling a C# project produces (DLL/EXE assemblies)
  - Basic compiler errors vs warnings and how to resolve common ones","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Data Types, Value vs Reference Semantics, and Memory Basics","scope_included":"- Understand built-in C# types and when to use them:
  - Numeric types (int, long, float, double, decimal) and their typical use cases
  - `bool`, `char`, `string`, `DateTime`, `TimeSpan`
  - Nullable value types (e.g., `int?`) and null checks
- Distinguish between value types and reference types at a practical level:
  - Understand that value types are copied on assignment and passed by value by default
  - Understand that reference types are references to objects on the heap
  - Recognize typical value types (`struct`, `enum`) and reference types (`class`, arrays, `string`)
- Work with arrays and basic data structures:
  - Declare, initialize, and iterate one-dimensional and simple multidimensional arrays
  - Understand array length vs capacity concepts
- Use basic type conversion and casting:
  - Implicit vs explicit casts for numeric types
  - `Convert` class usage and `Parse` / `TryParse` patterns for common types
  - Awareness of overflow and basic handling strategies
- Use `object` as the base type and understand boxing/unboxing at a conceptual level
- Understand basics of memory management in .NET:
  - Concept of managed heap and stack at a non-deep level
  - Role of the garbage collector and that developers do not manually free memory
  - Importance of releasing unmanaged resources via `using` / `IDisposable`","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Object-Oriented Programming in C#","scope_included":"- Apply core OOP principles in simple designs:
  - Encapsulation: use access modifiers (`public`, `private`, `internal`, `protected`) appropriately
  - Inheritance: derive classes from base classes and override virtual methods
  - Polymorphism: use virtual/override and interfaces to call through base types
  - Basic understanding of abstraction and separating interface from implementation
- Design and implement basic classes:
  - Fields, properties, methods, constructors, destructors (conceptual understanding)
  - Overloading methods and constructors
  - Using `this` keyword appropriately
- Implement and use interfaces:
  - Declare simple interfaces and implement them in classes
  - Program against interfaces in method signatures and variables
- Use inheritance wisely at a basic level:
  - Understand when inheritance vs composition is appropriate in simple scenarios
  - Use `base` keyword to call base class constructors and methods
- Use access modifiers to create minimal and safe public APIs for classes
- Understand sealed classes and methods at a basic conceptual level
- Recognize and avoid common anti-patterns at this level (e.g., excessive public fields, God classes in small components)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Collections and LINQ Basics","scope_included":"- Use primary collection types from `System.Collections.Generic`:
  - `List<T>` for ordered lists
  - `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` for key–value mappings
  - `HashSet<T>` and `Queue<T>` / `Stack<T>` at basic familiarity level
- Choose suitable collection types for common problems based on simple criteria (ordering, indexing, uniqueness)
- Perform common collection operations:
  - Adding, removing, searching, sorting elements
  - Iterating collections with `foreach` and indexed loops
- Use LINQ-to-Objects at a basic level:
  - Apply basic operators: `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `OrderByDescending`, `First`, `FirstOrDefault`, `SingleOrDefault`, `Take`, `Skip`
  - Chain multiple LINQ operators in simple queries
  - Understand deferred execution conceptually for LINQ queries
- Work with lambda expressions for LINQ and delegates:
  - Simple lambda syntax `(x => x.Property == value)`
  - Expression vs statement lambdas (basic recognition)
- Understand standard query operators vs query expression syntax and use at least one comfortably
- Avoid common pitfalls with LINQ at a basic level:
  - Checking for empty sequences before calling element operators
  - Awareness that some operators can throw (e.g., `Single`) and basic safe usage
- Materialize LINQ queries using `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary` at appropriate points","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Error Handling, Exceptions, and Diagnostics","scope_included":"- Use exceptions correctly in application code:
  - Throw and catch exceptions using `try` / `catch` / `finally`
  - Understand when to let exceptions bubble up vs catching locally
  - Catch specific exception types instead of broad `Exception` where possible
- Understand basic exception types in .NET:
  - `ArgumentException`, `ArgumentNullException`, `InvalidOperationException`, `NullReferenceException`, `FormatException`, `IOException` at a working level
- Create and use custom exception types in simple scenarios when needed
- Implement basic validation and guard clauses to prevent avoidable exceptions
- Use `finally` blocks and `using` statements to ensure cleanup of resources
- Log and surface errors appropriately for the application type (console, web, desktop) at a basic level
- Use basic debugging techniques:
  - Set breakpoints, step into/over, inspect variables, watch expressions in IDE
  - Inspect call stack and understand flow of execution through methods
- Read and interpret stack traces to locate the source of unhandled exceptions","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Delegates, Events, and Basic Functional Constructs","scope_included":"- Understand delegates at a practical level:
  - Concept that a delegate is a reference to a method signature
  - Use `Action`, `Func`, and `Predicate` built-in delegates
- Use lambda expressions with delegates and events for callback-style programming
- Understand and subscribe/unsubscribe to events:
  - Event declaration with `event` keyword at a basic recognition level
  - Event subscription using `+=` and unsubscription using `-=`
  - Handle common framework events (e.g., UI or .NET library events) in day-to-day coding
- Apply basic functional-style constructs:
  - Passing functions as parameters in simple APIs
  - Using LINQ with lambda expressions as a form of functional composition
- Recognize and avoid common pitfalls:
  - Avoid anonymous event handlers that cannot be unsubscribed when required
  - Basic awareness of event handlers as potential memory leak sources if not unsubscribed in long-lived contexts","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Asynchronous Programming and Multithreading (Basic Level)","scope_included":"- Understand the purpose of asynchrony in .NET:
  - Keeping applications responsive during I/O operations
  - Basic distinction between CPU-bound and I/O-bound work
- Use `async` / `await` in common scenarios:
  - Call asynchronous APIs provided by .NET or frameworks (e.g., HTTP calls, file I/O, DB I/O)
  - Correctly return `Task` or `Task<T>` from async methods
  - Avoid `async void` methods except in event handlers
- Basic understanding of `Task` and the task-based asynchronous pattern (TAP)
- Chain asynchronous operations in a simple, readable manner
- Recognize common issues at this level:
  - Avoid blocking calls on async methods (e.g., `.Result` / `.Wait()`) where it can cause deadlocks
  - Basic awareness that context capturing affects UI applications and ASP.NET
- Basic awareness of multithreading and the thread pool without deep mastery:
  - Understand that multiple threads may execute code simultaneously
  - Very basic understanding of race conditions and the need for synchronization constructs (not necessarily implementing complex ones)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":".NET Platform and Runtime Fundamentals","scope_included":"- Understand the .NET family at a conceptual level:
  - Difference between .NET (Core/5+) and older .NET Framework
  - Awareness of .NET as a cross-platform runtime for C# and other languages
- Understand CLR basics:
  - Role of the Common Language Runtime (CLR) in executing managed code
  - Concept of IL (Intermediate Language) and JIT compilation at a surface level
- Work with assemblies and namespaces:
  - Understanding of assemblies (DLLs/EXEs) as deployment units
  - Use namespaces to organize and reference types without conflicts
- Understand basic project organization in .NET:
  - Project vs solution structure
  - Class library projects vs executable projects
- Use and understand references:
  - Add and manage project references and NuGet package references
  - Basic understanding of versioning and compatibility concerns
- Awareness of .NET Standard and its purpose (compatibility between different .NET implementations) at a high level","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Application Development with .NET (Console, Web, and Desktop Basics)","scope_included":"- Develop simple console applications:
  - Use `Console` for input/output
  - Build small utilities or scripts that perform basic business logic or data processing
- Understand high-level application types in .NET:
  - Console, web (ASP.NET Core), desktop (WinForms/WPF), and service/background worker applications
  - Basic awareness of when each type is appropriate
- ASP.NET Core web application basics (if in web-focused roles):
  - Understanding of middleware pipeline at a conceptual level
  - Configure routing for simple endpoints
  - Build basic MVC or API controllers for CRUD-like operations
  - Model binding basics (binding from query string, route, and body)
  - Return common HTTP responses and status codes
- Desktop UI basics (if in desktop roles):
  - Work with basic forms/windows, controls, and event handlers (WinForms or WPF)
  - Implement simple data binding at an introductory level
- Basic configuration of application startup:
  - Know where the app starts and how execution flows through the main entry point or web startup pipeline
  - Understand environment-based configuration conceptually (Development, Staging, Production)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Data Access and Persistence Basics","scope_included":"- Understand general approaches to data access in .NET:
  - Direct database access (ADO.NET)
  - Object–relational mappers (ORMs) like Entity Framework Core
- ADO.NET basics:
  - Use `SqlConnection`, `SqlCommand`, and `SqlDataReader` for simple queries
  - Parameterized SQL commands to prevent basic SQL injection issues
  - Basic understanding of connection strings and their configuration
- Entity Framework Core basics (if used in environment):
  - Define simple entity classes and DbContext
  - Configure DbSets for entities
  - Perform basic CRUD operations (add, query, update, delete) via EF Core
  - Use basic migrations to evolve a schema (add migration, update database) with guidance
- Understand transactional concepts at a basic level:
  - Awareness of transactions for grouping database operations
  - Use transaction scopes or DbContext transactions in simple scenarios
- Map between domain models and persistence models for straightforward cases
- Handle and log common data access exceptions and errors","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Configuration, Logging, and Environment Management","scope_included":"- Use configuration in .NET applications:
  - Read configuration values from JSON files, environment variables, or other providers (especially in ASP.NET Core)
  - Bind configuration sections to simple C# objects (POCOs) in basic scenarios
- Store and access connection strings, API keys, and other settings securely at a basic level:
  - Awareness of sensitive data handling and avoiding hard-coded secrets in code
  - Basic familiarity with user secrets or environment variables
- Implement basic logging:
  - Use `ILogger` in ASP.NET Core or logging abstractions where available
  - Log at appropriate levels (Information, Warning, Error) for common events
  - Understand the importance of structured and meaningful log messages
- Adapt behavior based on environment:
  - Awareness of environment-specific configuration and how it affects application behavior
  - Basic strategies to toggle development vs production settings (e.g., detailed errors, verbose logging)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Dependency Management and Basic Dependency Injection","scope_included":"- Understand the concept of dependencies between components/classes
- Recognize problems caused by hard-coded dependencies in simple examples
- Understand dependency injection (DI) at an introductory level:
  - Concept of injecting dependencies via constructors or properties
  - Benefits: testability, flexibility, reduced coupling in simple terms
- Use built-in DI container in ASP.NET Core for basic scenarios:
  - Register services with lifetimes: transient, scoped, singleton (basic understanding of differences)
  - Resolve services through constructor injection
- Avoid service location pattern in new code at a basic awareness level
- Manage dependencies via interfaces and abstractions in simple architectures","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Architecture, Design Practices, and Code Quality (Basic Level)","scope_included":"- Understand basic layering in .NET applications:
  - Separate concerns between UI, business logic, and data access in simple projects
  - Recognize responsibilities of each layer at a high level
- Apply simple design principles:
  - Write small, focused methods and classes
  - Prefer composition over inheritance in straightforward scenarios
  - Avoid duplication by extracting reusable methods or classes
- Basic familiarity with SOLID at a conceptual level:
  - Especially Single Responsibility Principle and Interface Segregation in everyday tasks
- Understand and follow project coding standards and naming conventions
- Write readable and maintainable code:
  - Clear naming, minimal comments when code is self-explanatory
  - Avoid deeply nested conditionals by refactoring into smaller methods
- Perform basic refactoring with tools support:
  - Rename symbols, extract methods, extract interfaces, move classes
- Participate in and respond to code reviews:
  - Understand common feedback related to readability, simplicity, and correctness
  - Make iterative improvements based on review comments","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Testing Fundamentals in .NET","scope_included":"- Understand the role and value of automated tests in .NET development
- Write simple unit tests using a common test framework (e.g., xUnit, NUnit, or MSTest):
  - Arrange–Act–Assert pattern
  - Test simple classes and methods with clear inputs and outputs
- Use basic assertions to verify behavior and results
- Run tests via IDE test runner or command line (`dotnet test`)
- Use mocks or stubs at an introductory level (possibly via a mocking framework) to isolate dependencies
- Understand basic testing boundaries:
  - Unit vs integration tests at a conceptual level
  - What kinds of behavior should be covered by unit tests in simple scenarios
- Maintain tests alongside code:
  - Update tests when behavior changes
  - Avoid brittle tests by focusing on observable outcomes rather than implementation details","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Tooling: IDE, dotnet CLI, Build, and Package Management","scope_included":"- Use a primary .NET IDE effectively (Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code with C# extension):
  - Create, open, and navigate projects and solutions
  - Use IntelliSense, go-to-definition, and find-all-references features
  - Navigate between errors and warnings; use quick-fixes and code suggestions
- Use the `dotnet` CLI at a basic level:
  - Create new projects (`dotnet new`), restore packages, build, run, and test
  - Understand the role of the `.csproj` file and basic project configuration
- Manage NuGet packages:
  - Add, update, and remove packages using IDE or CLI (`dotnet add package`)
  - Understand semantic versioning at a basic level and choose appropriate package versions
- Work with build configurations:
  - Debug vs Release builds at a conceptual and practical level
  - Build and run applications locally for testing
- Use built-in analyzers and static code analysis tools at a basic level:
  - Address or suppress warnings responsibly when appropriate","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Source Control, Collaboration, and Documentation","scope_included":"- Use Git (or primary VCS) in day-to-day .NET development:
  - Clone repositories, create branches, commit changes, pull, and push
  - Resolve simple merge conflicts, especially in C# code and project files
- Follow team branching and merging strategies at a basic level (e.g., feature branches, pull requests)
- Participate in code reviews via pull requests:
  - Submit changes with clear descriptions
  - Respond to feedback and update code accordingly
- Write basic technical documentation for .NET components:
  - XML documentation comments on public methods and classes when required
  - Simple README or usage notes for small utilities or services
- Use work tracking tools (e.g., Azure DevOps, Jira, GitHub issues) to manage tasks and link work to code changes
- Communicate effectively with team members about technical changes, risks, and trade-offs at a straightforward level","is_non_core_section":true}]}
